analysis.one_liner: Requires advance notice before credit card rate hikes, bans fees for paying on time, and restricts cards for people under 21.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Financial Services Committee from May 2006 until that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced credit card companies to warn customers at least 15 days before raising their interest rate, and let customers pay off their balance at the old rate instead. It would have banned fees for paying on time or paying in full, banned over-the-limit fees on transactions the card company itself approved, and required statements to show how long and how much it would take to pay off a balance. It also would have barred most credit cards for people under 21 unless a parent co-signed or the person showed independent income.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders, especially people who carry balances and families with students. Rate hikes could no longer apply retroactively to existing balances, hidden fees for on-time or full payments would end, and college students under 21 would be protected from aggressive on-campus card marketing unless a parent or guardian co-signed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card holders and college students

how_it_helps.text: Card issuers would have to give at least 15 days' advance notice of an interest rate increase, and the increase could not apply to balances already owed — customers who cancel could pay off the old balance at the old rate [S2][S3].

The bill bans finance charges on amounts paid on time, penalties for paying a balance in full or paying more than the minimum, and over-the-limit fees on transactions the creditor approved in advance [S2][S3].

Statements would have to show, in a prominent table, how many months and what monthly payment would be needed to eliminate the balance in 36 months, plus the postmark deadline for avoiding late fees and any penalty interest rate [S2][S3].

No card could be issued to someone under 21 without a written application showing a co-signer, independent means of repayment, or completion of an approved nonprofit credit counseling course, and university affinity cards for students would face the same restrictions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which collect interest and fees — including retroactive rate increases, over-limit charges, and student-card revenue — would bear the cost of the banned practices and of reworking billing statements.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is cost-shifting: when regulators ban specific fees and retroactive rate increases, issuers may respond by raising rates for everyone, tightening approval, or adding annual fees, so careful borrowers can end up subsidizing the protections [S3].

The under-21 requirement would block young adults without a co-signer, documented income, or completed counseling from getting a card on their own, delaying independent credit access and credit history building [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are targeted at practices that were genuinely hard for cardholders to see or contest — retroactive rate hikes, fees for paying on time, and easy student cards. The main tradeoff is that some costs could be shifted to other cardholders and credit access for people under 21 would be harder. On balance, the bill's benefits to cardholders appear larger than its costs, though it is narrower than the comprehensive card reform Congress passed three years later.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2006 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never scheduled it for consideration, and the bill died there when that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Udall of Colorado introduced the Credit CARD Act of 2006 on May 11, 2006, with eight cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day it was introduced [S1].
The committee took no further action on the bill: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote appear in the action record before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].
The only later entries in the record are two statements by the sponsor entering introductory remarks in the Congressional Record, in May and July 2006 [S5].

A substantially similar set of credit card protections, including advance notice of rate increases and restrictions on cards for people under 21, was enacted three years later as the Credit CARD Act of 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers came out ahead: the fee and rate practices the bill targeted — retroactive rate increases, fees for on-time payments, over-limit fees, and easy student cards — continued unchanged for the rest of the Congress. Consumers who would have benefited from the protections waited until 2009.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers kept their practices

for.name: Mark Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and entered remarks promoting it in the Congressional Record twice after committee referral [S1][S5].

for.name: 8 of 202 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Bart Stupak, Tim Ryan, Julia Carson, Raúl Grijalva, Donna Christensen, and Ed Case [S3][S4].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the bill's record before the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Michael Oxley
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a markup or committee vote during the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats, and the committee that declined to act was controlled by Republicans in the 109th Congress; no Republicans signed on [S4].

industries.note: The bill bans several of their revenue practices — retroactive rate increases on existing balances, finance charges on timely payments, fees for paying in full, and over-limit fees on approved transactions — and adds liability exposure up to $5,000 per violation [S3]. Those fees came directly out of cardholders' pockets.

The bill restricts affinity card agreements between card issuers and higher education institutions, requiring the same under-21 protections for student cards [S3]. Universities earned marketing revenue from these deals while students picked up debt.
Agencies approved by the Federal Reserve would become an official pathway for under-21 applicants to qualify for credit cards, with conflict-of-interest and fee rules attached [S3].
